summary: A note from Bob Braden at UCLA's Campus Computing Network about the ASCII and EBCDIC mapping used by NETRJS, its remote job entry service. Users of ASCII hosts had found problems with the original mapping rules, so CCN changed the mapping and added a new one. The RFC tells users, alerts the RJE protocol committee, and acknowledges Joel Winett's earlier work.

eli5.summary: Two computers use different alphabets, so a translator swaps letters between them. This note says the translator's rules had mistakes, and explains how they were fixed.

questions: ebcdic to ascii mapping for network rje
subtitle: Character translation rules when ASCII terminals use an EBCDIC mainframe system

tldr.problem: NETRJS, a remote job entry system at UCLA, had to translate between ASCII (used on network computers) and EBCDIC (used on IBM mainframes), but the original character mapping rules had problems.
tldr.mechanism: Bob Braden updates the mapping rules based on earlier work by Joel Winett, creating special handling for six ASCII characters that do not exist in EBCDIC, and adds a special TTY mode for Model 33/35 Teletype terminals.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents the lessons learned and argues that servers should provide multiple translation tables to accommodate different terminal types rather than forcing users to adapt.

today: RFC 338 is part of the early history of character encoding on networks. Modern systems rely on standards like Unicode and UTF-8, which eliminate the need for this kind of mapping. However, the RFC's principle—that servers should adapt to client diversity rather than vice versa—remains relevant in protocol design.

sections.title: Character Translation in NETRJS
sections.content: NETRJS is UCLA's Network Remote Job Entry service, allowing remote terminals to submit batch jobs to UCLA's IBM 360/91 mainframe computer. The problem is that the mainframe internally uses EBCDIC character encoding, while most network-connected ASCII computers use ASCII. When an ASCII terminal connects to submit a job, the server must translate the incoming ASCII character stream to EBCDIC, execute the job in EBCDIC, and translate the output back to ASCII for the user to read.
sections.eli5: A big IBM computer speaks one character code, small network computers speak another. When they talk, NETRJS has to translate in both directions.

sections.title: Mapping the Characters
sections.content:
Bob Braden identifies the core requirement: map the 89 basic EBCDIC graphics into ASCII equivalents efficiently and transparently. For characters that exist in both sets, the best choice is to map them to themselves. This is not always possible—EBCDIC includes characters not in ASCII, like the cent sign and the bent bar, while ASCII includes brackets, braces, and backticks that do not exist in EBCDIC.

Earlier work by Joel Winett in RFC 183 established mapping rules. Braden adopts Winett's rules for the basic characters and addresses the remaining six "maverick" ASCII characters (brackets, braces, caret, and backtick) by mapping them to specific EBCDIC codes, rather than the original choice of translating them to question marks. This allows programmers to send true ASCII text to the mainframe for processing.
sections.eli5: Some letters are the same in both codes, so they map to themselves. Others exist in one code but not the other, so you have to pick an equivalent or invention a mapping.

sections.title: Terminal-Specific Mappings
sections.content: Beyond the standard ASCII and EBCDIC modes, Braden adds a third mode for Model 33/35 Teletypes, which have a different character set—including up-arrow and left-arrow keys in place of some ASCII graphics. The TTY mode uses yet another mapping to make the Teletype's character set usable with the EBCDIC mainframe. This solution demonstrates a key insight: rather than expecting users to adapt to a single translation table, the server should offer multiple tables to match different terminal types.
sections.eli5: Some old keyboards have weird keys instead of brackets or braces. So NETRJS added a special mode that translates those weird keys into the right EBCDIC codes.

sections.title: Lessons on Server Flexibility
sections.content: Braden concludes that one universal translation table cannot work. As users with different terminal types arrive on the network, the server must be prepared to provide a variety of translation tables and perhaps even allow users to specify their own. The broader lesson is that in a heterogeneous network, the server, not the user, should bear the burden of adaptation. This principle influenced later thinking about network protocol design and character encoding standards.
sections.eli5: This taught people that servers should be flexible about how they handle different keyboards and character sets, rather than making users figure it all out.

references.text: Braden, R. T., "Interim NETRJS Specifications", RFC 189, July 1971.
Winett, J., "The EBCDIC Codes and their Mapping to ASCII", RFC 183, July 1971.
